strengths: Introduces xRFM, a novel and practical combination of feature-learning kernel machines (RFM/AGOP) with adaptive tree partitioning, enabling local feature learning and scalability for tabular data.

Provides extensive empirical evaluation on TALENT, TabArena-Lite, and meta-test, comparing against 31+ methods including GBDTs, neural networks, and TabPFN-v2. xRFM achieves best regression performance on TALENT and competitive classification results, with strong large-scale results up to 500k samples.

Demonstrates strong scalability and efficiency: the tree-based design gives logarithmic inference time and near-linear training scaling, and xRFM lies on the empirical Pareto frontier for performance versus inference time on TabArena-Lite.
Offers native interpretability through leaf AGOPs, with qualitative examples on synthetic and real datasets showing plausible feature selection and local heterogeneity across leaves.
Reproducibility is supported by code availability, detailed algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameter search spaces, and metric definitions.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: xRFM combines prior RFM/AGOP feature learning with a simple median-split tree and tuned kernel-RFM leaves. Better positioning against prior tree/kernel hybrids and ablations isolating each component would strengthen the contribution.

Some claims appear overstated. On TabArena-Lite regression, tuned xRFM is not among the top three methods by Elo according to the full tables; it is below AutoGluon, RealMLP, ModernNCA, LightGBM, and TabDPT. The meta-test classification results also do not uniformly support 'best/second best' without more careful aggregation.

Computational complexity claims are imprecise. Leaf RFM solves kernel systems on leaves up to C=60,000, giving a large O(n C^2) cost with substantial constants, not simply O(n log n). No formal time/memory analysis or details of how large leaf kernel solves are made tractable are provided.

Interpretability evaluation is mostly qualitative. There is no quantitative comparison to SHAP, gradient-based importance, or tree feature importance, so the practical utility of AGOP as an interpretability mechanism is not rigorously established.

The paper lacks new theoretical guarantees for local feature learning, tree partitioning, or generalization. Empirical results are strong, but the central claims would benefit from formal analysis or more controlled synthetic experiments.

Benchmark fairness and tuning cost are not fully addressed. xRFM uses an extensive hyperparameter search space, while some baselines are default or tuned differently; TALENT runtime plots exclude tuning cost, which may affect efficiency comparisons.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: scalable, accurate, and interpretable learning on tabular data, where GBDTs remain dominant.
Extensive empirical evaluation across TALENT, TabArena-Lite, and meta-test benchmarks against many strong baselines, including GBDTs, neural methods, and TabPFN-v2.
The core high-level idea—combining RFM/AGOP-based feature learning with tree-based data partitioning—is reasonable and enables local feature learning, which is a promising direction for tabular data.
Reports strong regression performance and competitive classification performance, with code and hyperparameter tables provided, which aids reproducibility to some extent.
Interpretability via AGOP is an appealing native mechanism and is illustrated on several real and synthetic datasets.
weaknesses: Central scalability/complexity claims are unsupported or misleading. The abstract and introduction claim O(log n) inference, but each prediction requires evaluating the leaf RFM kernel against all training samples in the leaf, which can be up to C=60,000. Thus inference is O(C + log n), not O(log n), and the 'logarithmic inference' claim is technically false unless an unstated approximation is used.

Training-time claims are also incomplete. Leaf RFMs require solving kernel systems on leaves, potentially of size 60,000; direct solvers at this scale are infeasible on standard GPUs, yet no iterative/approximate solver is described for leaf RFM training. This undermines the O(n log n) scalability claim and creates a serious reproducibility gap.

Limited algorithmic novelty. The method largely combines existing RFM/AGOP feature learning with a balanced, median-split decision tree. Leaf RFM modifications—general K_{p,q} kernels, diagonal AGOP, adaptive bandwidth—are incremental and not theoretically analyzed.

No theoretical guarantees or analysis are provided for the tree partitioning, local feature learning, convergence, or generalization, despite making strong claims about feature learning and scalability.

Interpretability claims are weakly evaluated. The AGOP visualizations are qualitative, on a few datasets, with no quantitative validation, ground-truth feature recovery metric, user study, or comparison to established interpretability methods such as SHAP or tree-based feature importance.

Some reported claims are inconsistent with the paper’s own tables. For example, the text says tuned xRFM is 'among the top three methods for regression' on TabArena-Lite, but Table B.8 ranks xRFM (T+E) around 6th by Elo and 11.5th by average rank, below AutoGluon, RealMLP, ModernNCA, LightGBM, and TabDPT.

Evaluation fairness is unclear. xRFM uses extensive per-leaf hyperparameter tuning, per-leaf validation, and many tuned kernel choices, while runtime comparisons appear to exclude tuning time. This may advantage xRFM relative to baselines with different tuning budgets.

Missing ablations: there is no systematic ablation isolating the effects of tree partitioning, leaf RFM iterations, diagonal AGOP, adaptive bandwidth, and kernel choice. The tradeoff controlled by leaf size C is not analyzed.

Reproducibility and compute details are insufficient: the leaf RFM solver, split-model subsample size, validation splitting strategy, tuning budgets, and compute resources are not fully specified, making it difficult to reproduce the scalability claims.

strengths: Introduces xRFM, a novel and practical method that combines feature-learning kernel machines (RFM) with tree-based partitioning, enabling local feature learning and scalability to large tabular datasets.

Strong empirical evaluation across three benchmarks: best regression performance on TALENT among 31 methods, competitive classification, Pareto-optimal trade-off on TabArena-Lite, and strong results on large meta-test datasets.
Provides natural interpretability through AGOP matrices, with qualitative examples showing sensible feature recovery on real tabular datasets.
Addresses scalability with O(n log n) training and O(log n) inference, supported by runtime experiments and comparisons to KRR/RFM.
Extensive hyperparameter search spaces and detailed appendix; code with scikit-learn-style API supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The method is largely heuristic and lacks theoretical guarantees for the tree partitioning, local feature learning, or AGOP-based interpretability; its success is primarily empirical.

Some claims are slightly overstrong: e.g., 'essentially unlimited amounts of training data' is only demonstrated up to 500K samples, and 'top three' on TabArena-Lite regression is not clearly supported by the Elo table.
Interpretability is only demonstrated qualitatively on four datasets; no quantitative comparison to established feature-importance methods (e.g., SHAP) or user study is provided.

Reproducibility details for the split model are incomplete: the subsample size used for AGOP-based splitting is not clearly specified in the main text or hyperparameter table, and its impact on performance/runtime is not ablated.

The comparison protocol may not fully account for hyperparameter tuning costs, as TALENT plots report runtime for the best configuration only; fairness relative to default/tuned baselines is not fully transparent.

strengths: Combines feature-learning kernel machines (RFM) with adaptive tree partitioning to enable local feature learning and scalability for tabular data, a novel and practically relevant direction.
Strong empirical results: best performance on 100 TALENT regression datasets, competitive on 200 classification datasets, and competitive against 31+ strong baselines including TabPFN-v2 and GBDTs.
Extensive evaluation across TALENT, TabArena-Lite, and large meta-test datasets, including datasets up to 500k samples, with extensive tables and significance tests for key comparisons.
Demonstrates favorable inference-time tradeoffs and Pareto-optimal behavior on TabArena-Lite, making the method attractive for practical tabular ML pipelines.
Provides native interpretability via AGOP with illustrative examples on real datasets such as California Housing, Covertype, NYC Taxi, and Breast Cancer.
Detailed appendix includes algorithms, hyperparameter search spaces, additional benchmark results, and split-method ablations, supporting reproducibility and transparency.
Addresses an important open problem: improving over GBDT dominance in tabular data with a scalable, feature-learning kernel approach.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: xRFM largely combines existing RFM feature learning with tree-based partitioning; no formal analysis or guarantees are provided for the local feature-learning or scalability claims.

Reproducibility concerns: the manuscript's code link is missing in the provided text, and the solver used for leaf RFM on up to 60k samples is not specified, making it hard to assess computational feasibility or reproduce training.

The interpretability evaluation is qualitative and illustrative only; there is no quantitative comparison to established interpretability methods such as SHAP, permutation importance, or tree-based feature importance.

The scalability claim of scaling to 'essentially unlimited' data is overstated; actual behavior depends on fixed leaf size, constant factors, and hyperparameter tuning overhead not included in runtime comparisons.
Some baseline comparisons may be imperfect: TabPFN-v2 is subsampled to 10k samples due to OOM, and TALENT baselines may not have been tuned with exactly the same search budget as xRFM.
Ablations are limited; there is little systematic exploration of leaf size, split-sample size, sensitivity to kernel choices, or the precise benefit of local feature learning.
No discussion of ethical, fairness, privacy, or bias implications, which is especially relevant for tabular data that may contain sensitive attributes.
The paper overclaims in places (e.g., 'best performance across 100 regression datasets' without qualifying it as TALENT-specific, and 'essentially unlimited amounts of training data').

strengths: Combines feature-learning kernel machines (RFM/AGOP) with a tree-based partitioning scheme, enabling local feature learning and scalable routing.
Reports strong empirical performance on the TALENT regression benchmark and competitive results on several classification benchmarks, with extensive appendix results.
The proposed leaf-RFM modifications (general Lp^q kernels, diagonal AGOP, categorical handling, adaptive bandwidth) are practical and well-motivated.
Provides an interpretability route via leaf-level AGOP matrices, with qualitative examples on real and synthetic datasets.
The algorithm is described with sufficient detail for implementation, including pseudocode and hyperparameter search spaces.
weaknesses: Evaluation against TabPFN-v2 is not apples-to-apples: TabPFN-v2 is subsampled to 10,000 samples on TALENT due to memory restrictions, while xRFM uses the full data, undermining the claim that xRFM outperforms the current tabular foundation model.

The paper overclaims on TabArena-Lite: xRFM is described as 'among the top three' for regression, but the reported Elo/normalized scores place it around 5th-6th or worse, with several methods clearly ahead.
Reproducibility is compromised by the missing code link in the abstract ('available at: .'), which is critical for a new algorithm with many hyperparameters.
Runtime comparisons largely exclude hyperparameter tuning cost and report only the best configuration per dataset, which may substantially overstate xRFM's practical efficiency relative to baselines.

Interpretability claims are supported only by qualitative examples; there is no quantitative evaluation or comparison against established feature-importance methods such as SHAP, permutation importance, or tree-based importance.

Novelty is incremental: the work combines existing RFM/AGOP feature learning with standard tree-based partitioning, and does not provide theoretical guarantees for the split procedure or local feature learning.

Scalability claims such as scaling to 'essentially unlimited amounts of training data' are not supported, as experiments go up to only 500k samples and the complexity argument relies on a fixed leaf size.
Some benchmark claims are inconsistent across sections; for example, classification rankings and TabArena performance statements are stronger than what the full tables actually show.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated combination of kernel Recursive Feature Machines with adaptive tree partitioning, enabling local feature learning and scalability to large tabular datasets.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three major tabular benchmarks (TALENT, TabArena-Lite, meta-test), including hundreds of datasets and strong baselines such as TabPFN-v2, GBDTs, and modern neural networks.
Achieves best or competitive performance on TALENT regression and competitive classification results, with strong evidence for Pareto-optimal inference/performance tradeoffs on TabArena-Lite.
Includes several practical algorithmic optimizations for tabular data, e.g., general L_p^q kernels, diagonal AGOP, categorical speedups, and adaptive bandwidth selection.
Provides native interpretability through AGOP, with illustrative examples on synthetic and real datasets showing locally learned features.
Good reproducibility: code is available with a scikit-learn-style API, and the appendix provides detailed algorithms, hyperparameter search spaces, and results tables.
weaknesses: The core novelty is largely a combination of existing RFM and tree-based partitioning; no formal theoretical analysis is provided for the claimed O(n log n) training, O(log n) inference, or the local feature learning benefit.

Some claims are overstated. For example, on TabArena-Lite regression, xRFM has Elo rank 11.5, not 'top three' by standard performance metrics, though it is competitive on the performance/runtime Pareto frontier.
Interpretability is evaluated only qualitatively; there is no quantitative comparison to established feature importance methods such as SHAP, permutation importance, or tree-based importance scores.
Ablations do not fully isolate the contribution of individual leaf-RFM modifications (e.g., diagonal AGOP, L_p^q kernels, adaptive bandwidth, categorical optimizations).
Despite discussing scalable kernel approximations such as Nyström, Falkon, and EigenPro, the paper does not compare against these methods end-to-end on the tabular benchmarks.
The split-model hyperparameter tuning procedure and total tuning budget are not fully specified, raising potential fairness concerns relative to extensively tuned baselines.
Per-leaf hyperparameter tuning and many leaf models can incur substantial memory/compute overhead, and no explicit limitations section discusses this or other practical constraints.
